title: Pokémon & Monster-Collecting
blurb: Pokémon arrived in Europe late, but it defined the Game Boy Color here. <cite>Pokémon Gold</cite> surely defined my life at 11 years old! This chapter collects the second generation, its spin-offs and the monster-collecting games that followed it.

games.title: Dragon Warrior Monsters
games.blurb: Enix’s monster-breeding RPG was known in Japan and non-English-speaking European countries as <cite>Dragon Quest Monsters</cite>. Eidos brought it to Europe in January 2000, which made it the first Dragon Quest game ever released here. It has 215 monsters, and stars Terry and Milly from <cite>Dragon Quest VI</cite> as children.

games.title: Pokémon Pinball
games.blurb: This one includes two tables, red and blue, and 151 Pokémon to catch by hitting the right targets. The cartridge has its own rumble motor, powered by a separate AAA battery, which made it a bit top-heavy! Europe got the game in October 2000, more than a year after America.

games.title: Pokémon Trading Card Game
games.blurb: The card game on a cartridge, known in Japan as <cite>Pokémon Card GB</cite>. It has 226 cards, some of which never existed in the real card game. Trading over infrared unlocks extra cards through “Card Pop!”. Europe got it in December 2000, two years after Japan.

games.title: Pokémon Gold and Silver
games.blurb: Likely my most played Game Boy Color game! The second generation, with a new region called Johto, a day and night cycle, and breeding. Together they sold over 23 million copies, more than any other Game Boy Color game. Europe got them on 6 April 2001, almost a year and a half after Japan.

games.title: Pokémon Puzzle Challenge
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Pokémon de Panepon</cite>, it’s really just a <cite>Panel de Pon</cite> type game, similar to <cite>Tetris Attack</cite>. Interestingly, the N64 counterpart <cite>Pokémon Puzzle League</cite> is based on the anime, while this GBC game is based on <cite>Gold and Silver</cite>. Europe got it in June 2001.

games.title: Pokémon Crystal
games.blurb: The definitive version of <cite>Gold and Silver</cite>, with animated sprites, a Battle Tower and (for the first time) a female playable character option. It was also the first Pokémon game that doesn’t run on the original DMG. The Japanese version could connect to mobile phones, but that feature never came to Europe.

games.title: Hamtaro: Ham-Hams Unite!
games.blurb: Based on the <cite>Hamtaro</cite> anime: Hamtaro gathers his friends by learning “Ham-Chat” words. It was the last Game Boy Color game Nintendo ever published. Europe got it in January 2003. <cite>Eurogamer</cite> and <cite>IGN</cite> said it works for adults as well as children, and I agree!

games.title: Yu-Gi-Oh! Dark Duel Stories
games.blurb: A card-battle game based on the <cite>Yu-Gi-Oh!</cite> anime. In Japan it was called <cite>Duel Monsters III</cite>. Europe got it in March 2003, a year after America. The Japanese game called <cite>Dark Duel Stories</cite> was actually a different game that never left Japan.

title: Mario, Zelda & Wario
blurb: Nintendo’s own games on the Game Boy Color: three Zelda adventures, a Mario classic in colour, Wario’s strangest platformer and two Game & Watch collections.

games.title: Game & Watch Gallery 2
games.blurb: Six Game & Watch games, each in a classic version and a modern version starring Mario and friends. In Japan it was <cite>Game Boy Gallery 2</cite>, a 1997 Game Boy game. Europe got the colour version on 3 December 1998, the same day as <cite>Tetris DX</cite>.

games.title: Game & Watch Gallery 3
games.blurb: Five more Game & Watch games in classic and modern versions, plus six classics to unlock. In Japan it was <cite>Game Boy Gallery 3</cite>, and in Australia <cite>Game Boy Gallery 4</cite>. Europe got it in March 2000.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening DX
games.blurb: The 1993 Game Boy adventure in colour, with a new Colour Dungeon full of colour-based puzzles that only opens on a Game Boy Color. A photo album lets you print pictures as stickers on the Game Boy Printer. Europe got it in February 1999.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Ages
games.blurb: One half of a linked pair, made by Capcom’s Flagship studio. <cite>Ages</cite> is about travelling through time and leans towards puzzles. A password from one game carries over into the other, and finishing both unlocks the real ending. Europe got both games on 4 October 2001.

games.title: The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Seasons
games.blurb: The other half of the pair, built around changing the seasons, and more focused on combat. The two <cite>Oracle</cite> games sold 3.99 million copies together.

games.title: Super Mario Bros. Deluxe
games.blurb: The 1985 NES game on a handheld, with new challenge and race modes. It also hides <cite>The Lost Levels</cite>, the Japanese sequel, as an unlockable extra. It stayed in the sales charts for two years. Europe got it in June 1999.

games.title: Wario Land 3
games.blurb: Wario is trapped inside a music box and cannot die: enemies only change his shape or his abilities. Day and night change the levels, and there are 100 treasures to find. Europe got it on 13 April 2000, more than six weeks before America.

title: Platformers
blurb: Platformers from Rare, Capcom, Hudson Soft and Ubi Soft, including two Rayman games and a <cite>Donkey Kong Country</cite> that Europe got before anyone else.

games.title: Conker’s Pocket Tales
games.blurb: Conker the Squirrel’s first game, two years before the N64 game made him famous. He searches for his stolen birthday presents and his kidnapped girlfriend, Berri. The cartridge also runs on the original Game Boy and the Super Game Boy. Europe got it in July 1999.

games.title: Pocket Bomberman
games.blurb: A Bomberman platformer instead of a maze game, with a Jump Mode where Bomberman bounces through the levels. It first came out in Japan in 1997 as a monochrome Game Boy game. The colour version reached Europe in 1999.

games.title: Donkey Kong Country
games.blurb: Rare’s SNES game on the Game Boy Color. Rare built it alongside the GBC <cite>Perfect Dark</cite>, and reused graphics and sound from the <cite>Donkey Kong Land</cite> games. Europe got it on 16 November 2000, before America and Japan.

games.title: Rayman
games.blurb: Ubi Soft’s limbless hero on the Game Boy Color, converted by Digital Eclipse. It uses the “Ubi Key”: Ubi Soft games could unlock bonuses in each other over the infrared port. Europe got it in July 2000.

games.title: Rayman 2 Forever
games.blurb: Europe’s title for the handheld <cite>Rayman 2</cite>. America called it <cite>Rayman 2: The Great Escape</cite>, like the console game. It was made by Ubi Soft’s studio in Milan, and Europe got it on 14 December 2001, a few weeks before America.

games.title: Croc 2
games.blurb: A 2D version of the 3D <cite>Croc 2</cite> from British studio Argonaut, rebuilt for the handheld by Natsume. Europe got it in February 2001, about a week after America.

games.title: Mega Man Xtreme
games.blurb: A handheld spin-off of the SNES <cite>Mega Man X</cite> series, known in Japan as <cite>Rockman X: Cyber Mission</cite>. Europe got it in August 2001.

games.title: Mega Man Xtreme 2
games.blurb: The sequel, known in Japan as <cite>Rockman X: Soul Eraser</cite>, set between <cite>Mega Man X3</cite> and <cite>X4</cite>. It sold 88,564 copies in Japan in 2001. Europe got it in February 2002.

title: Action, Stealth & Horror
blurb: Stealth, shooting and survival horror on a small screen. Several of these games were made for Europe, or reached Europe first.

games.title: Duke Nukem
games.blurb: A port of the 1993 PC game <cite>Duke Nukem II</cite>, with Duke fighting the Rigelatins across side-scrolling levels. Neo LA from the PC version became Nerola City. Europe got it in September 1999, at the same time as America.

games.title: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors’ Dreams
games.blurb: British studio Crawfish converted Capcom’s arcade fighter, without a link-cable mode. Europe got it on 17 December 1999, three months before America. Even the Japanese release used the Western name <cite>Alpha</cite> instead of <cite>Zero</cite>.

games.title: Metal Gear Solid
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Metal Gear: Ghost Babel</cite>. It is not a port of the PlayStation game, but a new story built for the handheld. Konami’s European branch asked for a Game Boy Color <cite>Metal Gear Solid</cite>, and with 95.61% it is the best-rated Game Boy Color game on GameRankings. Europe got it on 1 May 2000.

games.title: Perfect Dark
games.blurb: A prequel to the N64 game: Joanna Dark finishes her training at the Carrington Institute and uncovers dataDyne’s plans. Europe got it in September 2000, a few days after America.

games.title: Tomb Raider
games.blurb: Lara Croft’s first handheld game, made by British studio Core Design. It began as a prototype for a science-fiction project called “Salvage”, and is also known as <cite>Tomb Raider: The Nightmare Stone</cite>. Europe got it in June 2000.

games.title: Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare
games.blurb: A handheld version of Infogrames’ survival-horror game, made separately by British studio Pocket Studios. Europe got it on 18 May 2001, a month before America. <cite>GamesMaster</cite> gave it 90%.

games.title: Resident Evil Gaiden
games.blurb: Virgin Interactive, Capcom’s European publisher, asked British studio M4 to make it. You explore from above, and fights switch to a first-person view. Europe got it on 14 December 2001, months before Japan and America.

games.title: Return of the Ninja
games.blurb: A stealth platformer, and a spiritual successor to Natsume’s <cite>Shadow of the Ninja</cite> on the NES. Europe got it on 30 March 2001, two months before America.

title: RPGs, Farms & Fishing
blurb: Few Japanese RPGs reached Europe on the Game Boy Color, so this chapter mixes RPGs with the farming and fishing games that did.

games.title: Bomberman Quest
games.blurb: An action RPG in which Bomberman fights monsters and the bosses of each area. It was the last Bomberman game by composer Jun Chikuma. Europe got it in May 1999, half a year before America.

games.title: Harvest Moon GB
games.blurb: The first handheld Harvest Moon, released in Europe as <cite>Harvest Moon GB</cite> and in America as <cite>Harvest Moon GBC</cite>. Nintendo published it in Europe in November 1999.

games.title: Harvest Moon 2 GBC
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Bokujō Monogatari GB2</cite>. The goal is to save the farm before the land is turned into an amusement park, and you can play as a boy or a girl. Europe got it in March 2001.

games.title: Azure Dreams
games.blurb: A dungeon crawler about climbing the Monster Tower with monsters you hatch yourself. Compared with the PlayStation original, it has more than twice as many monsters and an extra 100-floor dungeon, but no town building or dating. Europe got it in 2000.

games.title: Legend of the River King GB
games.blurb: A fishing RPG: a boy catches fish to find the Guardian Fish that can cure his sick sister. It was the first <cite>Kawa no Nushi Tsuri</cite> game released in the West, and Europe’s title added “GB”. Europe got it in December 2000, more than a year after America.

games.title: Legend of the River King 2
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Kawa no Nushi Tsuri 4</cite>. Europe got it on 30 March 2001, a few weeks before America.

games.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone
games.blurb: A turn-based RPG, instead of the action game on other systems. Europe got it on 16 November 2001 under the book’s original British title, a day after America got <cite>Sorcerer’s Stone</cite>.

games.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
games.blurb: Griptonite’s second Harry Potter RPG, again turn-based and again different from the console versions. Europe got it on 15 November 2002.

games.title: Lufia: The Legend Returns
games.blurb: The first handheld <cite>Lufia</cite>, with randomly generated dungeons. Ubi Soft published it in Europe in October 2001.

title: Puzzle
blurb: Falling blocks, popping bubbles and a few puzzle games from British and Scottish studios.

games.title: Tetris DX
games.blurb: <cite>Tetris</cite> in colour, with save files, new modes and a two-player mode over the link cable. Europe got it on 3 December 1998, as one of the first Game Boy Color games released here.

games.title: Hexcite: The Shapes of Victory
games.blurb: A puzzle game about placing shapes on a hexagonal board. It was a launch game for the Game Boy Color in Japan, and Landwarf reworked it for the West. Europe got it in January 1999.

games.title: Bust-A-Move Millennium
games.blurb: Known in Japan as <cite>Puzzle Bobble Millennium</cite>: aim, fire and pop bubbles of the same colour. Europe got it in November 2000.

games.title: Mr. Driller
games.blurb: Namco’s arcade puzzle game: drill down through coloured blocks before your air runs out. Europe and America got it on the same day, 2 August 2000.

games.title: Puchi Carat
games.blurb: A puzzle game based on Taito’s 1997 arcade original. Europe got it in December 2000, but America never did.

games.title: Wetrix GB
games.blurb: A water puzzle game by British studio Zed Two, run by brothers Ste and John Pickford. You raise the landscape with falling pieces to hold water. Japan got it first, and Europe followed in September 2000.

games.title: Denki Blocks!
games.blurb: A puzzle game by Scottish studio Denki: slide coloured blocks around a grid to join them. <cite>Edge</cite> said it felt as if it was made in Kyoto rather than Aberdeen. Rage published it in September 2001.

title: Sports & Racing
blurb: Football, rallying, touring cars and kart racing, from studios in Britain, France, Spain and Japan.

games.title: International Track & Field
games.blurb: Konami’s button-mashing athletics game, known in Japan as <cite>Hyper Olympic Track & Field GB</cite>. Europe got it in November 1999, two months before America.

games.title: Mario Golf
games.blurb: Camelot’s handheld companion to the N64 <cite>Mario Golf</cite>. Europe got it in the autumn of 1999.

games.title: Mickey’s Racing Adventure
games.blurb: A kart racer by Rare, starring Mickey Mouse and friends. Over infrared, it unlocks a secret track in <cite>Mickey’s Speedway USA</cite>. Europe got it in late 1999, days after America.

games.title: V-Rally: Championship Edition
games.blurb: Europe’s title for <cite>V-Rally: Edition ’99</cite>, the handheld version of Infogrames’ rally series from Lyon. It was converted by Bit Managers in Barcelona. Europe and America got it in June 1999.

games.title: 4x4 World Trophy
games.blurb: Europe’s title for <cite>Test Drive Off-Road 3</cite>. The cartridge has a built-in rumble feature. Europe got it in April 2000, five months after America.

games.title: International Superstar Soccer 2000
games.blurb: Konami’s football game, known in Japan as <cite>World Soccer GB 2000</cite>. Europe got it in September 2000, months before America.

games.title: Micro Machines 1 and 2: Twin Turbo
games.blurb: Codemasters’ top-down racers, both on one cartridge, converted by British studio Virtucraft. Europe and America got it in 2000.

games.title: Supercross Freestyle
games.blurb: A motocross game by French duo Fernando Velez and Guillaume Dubail, with racing, freestyle tricks and an arcade mode. It was only released in Europe. <cite>CVG</cite> put it “on the podium” for best Game Boy racer ever.

games.title: Xtreme Wheels
games.blurb: A BMX racer that reviewers compared to <cite>Excitebike</cite>. Europe got it in November 2000, five months before America.

games.title: Colin McRae Rally
games.blurb: The first handheld <cite>Colin McRae Rally</cite>, released only in Europe, in 2001.

games.title: Mario Tennis
games.blurb: Camelot’s companion to the N64 game, with a story mode called Mario Tour. Europe got it on 1 February 2001.

games.title: TOCA Touring Car Championship
games.blurb: Codemasters’ touring-car series on the Game Boy Color, made by Spellbound. Europe got it in November 2001.

title: Licensed & TV Tie-ins
blurb: Film, TV and toy licences, several of them British or French: <cite>Chicken Run</cite>, <cite>Robot Wars</cite>, <cite>Thunderbirds</cite> and <cite>Kirikou</cite>.

games.title: Tarzan
games.blurb: The Game Boy Color version of Disney’s <cite>Tarzan</cite>, made by Digital Eclipse, a studio best known for faithful ports such as <cite>Joust</cite> and <cite>Paperboy</cite>. Europe and America got it in June 1999.

games.title: Austin Powers: Oh, Behave! and Welcome to My Underground Lair!
games.blurb: Two cartridges, one for Austin Powers and one for Dr. Evil, that can connect to each other. Rockstar Games published them, and Europe got both on 3 November 2000. Two more games were planned but never released.

games.title: Chicken Run
games.blurb: Based on Aardman’s British film. On the Game Boy Color it is an isometric puzzle game: Ginger lures the other chickens to the exit with corn. Europe got it in November 2000.

games.title: Robot Wars: Metal Mayhem
games.blurb: The first game based on the British TV show <cite>Robot Wars</cite>, released only on the Game Boy Color. It is based on the third series, with champion Chaos 2. BBC Multimedia published it on 7 December 2000.

games.title: Spider-Man
games.blurb: A Game Boy Color original by Vicarious Visions. It got a sequel that was only released on the Game Boy Color, <cite>Spider-Man 2: The Sinister Six</cite>. Europe got it in September 2000.

games.title: Thunderbirds
games.blurb: SCi bought the <cite>Thunderbirds</cite> licence when BBC Two brought back the 1965 series in 2000. <cite>Total Game Boy</cite> called it “a ripping adventure”. It came out in Europe only, in December 2000.

games.title: Action Man: Search for Base X
games.blurb: Based on the <cite>Action Man</cite> TV series and toy line. Europe got it in March 2001, a month after America.

games.title: Kirikou
games.blurb: Based on Michel Ocelot’s French animated film <cite>Kirikou and the Sorceress</cite>. Wanadoo published it in Europe in November 2001, together with PlayStation and PC versions.

games.title: Dragon Ball Z: Legendary Super Warriors
games.blurb: A turn-based card-battle game that covers the anime from the Saiyan Saga to the Buu Saga. Europe got it in 2002.

title: Comic Heroes from Europe
blurb: Europe’s comic heroes, from Belgium, France, Switzerland and Finland. Most of these games were only released in Europe, and several were made by European studios.

games.title: Lucky Luke
games.blurb: A colour version of the 1997 Game Boy game, based on the Belgian comic. Europe got it in May 1999, and it was one of the few European comic games that also reached America.

games.title: Astérix: Search for Dogmatix
games.blurb: Asterix and Obelix go looking for their dog, Dogmatix. It was made by British studio Rebellion and published by Infogrames. Europe got it in May 2000, and it never came out in America.

games.title: Moomin’s Tale
games.blurb: Based on Tove Jansson’s Moomins from Finland. Sunsoft published it in Japan in June 2000, and Europe got it in December 2000.

games.title: Papyrus
games.blurb: Based on Lucien De Gieter’s Belgian comic, which first ran in <cite>Spirou</cite> magazine in 1974. Ubi Soft announced it at ECTS as a Europe-only release, and it came out in February 2000.

games.title: The Smurfs’ Nightmare
games.blurb: Gargamel traps the Smurfs in their nightmares, and one Smurf has to rescue the others. It came in English, French, German and Spanish. Pirates later hacked it into a fake Pokémon game called <cite>Monster Go! Go! Go!</cite>. Europe got it in 2000.

games.title: Spirou: The Robot Invasion
games.blurb: Known in French as <cite>Spirou : La Panique mécanique</cite>, and a follow-up to the 1996 Game Boy <cite>Spirou</cite>. German <cite>Total!</cite> gave it 1.75 on a scale where 1 is the best. Europe got it in 2000.

games.title: Tintin: Le Temple du Soleil
games.blurb: A colour version of the 1997 <cite>Prisoners of the Sun</cite> game, based on the albums <cite>The Seven Crystal Balls</cite> and <cite>Prisoners of the Sun</cite>. Bit Managers made it, and it came out in Europe in September 2000.

games.title: Titeuf
games.blurb: A party game based on Swiss cartoonist Zep’s schoolboy, known in English as Tootuff. Infogrames released it in France in June 2001.

games.title: Suske en Wiske: De Tijdtemmers
games.blurb: Willy Vandersteen’s Flemish comic heroes, known in French as <cite>Bob et Bobette</cite>. Dutch studio Witan made it, with graphics by Engine Software and music by Jeroen Tel of Maniacs of Noise. Infogrames Benelux released it in 2002.

title: Arcade Classics & Shooters
blurb: Arcade games from Konami, Namco, Taito, Capcom, Irem and Midway, converted for the Game Boy Color, several of them by British studios.

games.title: Frogger
games.blurb: Konami’s 1981 arcade game: get the frogs safely across the road and the river. Majesco published it in America in December 1998, and Europe got it in 1999.

games.title: Pac-Man: Special Colour Edition
games.blurb: Released for Pac-Man’s 20th anniversary, with <cite>Pac-Attack</cite>, a falling-block puzzle game, on the same cartridge. Acclaim published it in Europe in August 1999, with “Colour” in the title.

games.title: Ms. Pac-Man: Special Colour Edition
games.blurb: The arcade sequel in colour. Acclaim published it in Europe in November 1999.

games.title: Rampage 2: Universal Tour
games.blurb: Giant monsters smash their way through cities around the world. Digital Eclipse converted it, and Europe got it in November 1999.

games.title: R-Type DX
games.blurb: Both Game Boy <cite>R-Type</cite> games on one cartridge, in colour, made by British studio Bits. Europe got it on 20 July 1999.

games.title: Space Invaders
games.blurb: A colour version of Taito’s arcade classic, made by British studio Crawfish and published by Activision. Japan called it <cite>Space Invaders X</cite>. Europe and America got it in October 1999.
Capcom’s 1984 arcade shooter, converted by Digital Eclipse. Europe got it in 2001, months after America.

games.title: Ghosts ’n Goblins
games.blurb: Capcom’s arcade classic, based on the NES version, with passwords to skip to later levels. Europe got it in August 2001, a year and a half after America.

title: Home-Computer Hits
blurb: Europe grew up on home computers, and many of their hits came to the Game Boy Color. This chapter collects them.

games.title: Grand Theft Auto
games.blurb: The first <cite>Grand Theft Auto</cite>, from Scottish studio DMA Design, on a handheld. Rockstar released it in Europe on 22 October 1999, a month before America.

games.title: Cannon Fodder
games.blurb: Sensible Software’s war game from the Amiga, converted by Codemasters. Europe got it in November 2000, before America.

games.title: Carmageddon
games.blurb: The controversial British PC game, converted by Aqua Pacific. SCi published it in Europe in April 2000.

games.title: Die Original Moorhuhn Jagd
games.blurb: The German PC shooting game, in which you shoot chickens. Ravensburger Interactive released the Game Boy Color version in 2000.

games.title: Worms Armageddon
games.blurb: Team17’s artillery game, rebuilt for the handheld. Europe got it in 2000.

games.title: Commander Keen
games.blurb: A new <cite>Commander Keen</cite>, ten years after the MS-DOS episodes. The idea came from John Carmack and id Software, who approached Activision. Europe got it in June 2001.

games.title: Heroes of Might and Magic II
games.blurb: A handheld version of the PC strategy game. Europe got it in March 2001.

games.title: SWIV
games.blurb: The Sales Curve’s vertically scrolling shooter from the Amiga and Atari ST. SCi published the Game Boy Color version in Europe in March 2001.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: The odd, the rare and the overlooked, including several games that were only released in Europe.

games.title: Space Station Silicon Valley
games.blurb: A 2D version of DMA Design’s N64 game, made by Tarantula Studios. It came out in Europe in July 1999.

games.title: Stranded Kids
games.blurb: A survival game on a deserted island, known in America as <cite>Survival Kids</cite>. The series later became <cite>Lost in Blue</cite>. Europe got it in December 1999.

games.title: Alfred’s Adventure
games.blurb: A remake of the Game Boy <cite>Alfred Chicken</cite>, made by Möbius Entertainment and released only in Europe. SCi published it in 2000.

games.title: Hype: The Time Quest
games.blurb: Based on Playmobil’s knights and castles. Ubi Soft released it in Europe in September 2000, while America waited more than a year.

games.title: John Romero’s Daikatana
games.blurb: Not a shooter like the PC game, but a top-down action adventure. Kemco cancelled the American release, and Japan only got it as a download. Europe got it on cartridge in September 2000.

games.title: Konami GB Collection Vol. 4
games.blurb: Four older Konami Game Boy games on one cartridge, in colour. Japan had monochrome versions in 1997 and 1998, but the colour versions of all four volumes were only released in Europe. IGN gave it eight out of ten.

games.title: Toki Tori
games.blurb: A puzzle platformer by Dutch studio Two Tribes, published by Capcom: a chick collects eggs with a limited set of tools. Europe got it in March 2002, half a year after America.
